difficultyReason: Two-premise argument with several topically related distractors. The gap between the pharmacological evidence and the conclusion requires ruling out an alternative explanation. Negation test discriminates cleanly.
stimulus: Neurologist: Patients with chronic migraines who were given compound X reported a significant reduction in headache frequency within four weeks. No other changes were made to their diet or medication regimens during this period. We therefore conclude that compound X is effective at reducing the frequency of chronic migraines.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the neurologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compound X has no side effects that would prevent patients from completing a four-week treatment course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reduction in headache frequency was not the result of patients' expectations of improvement rather than any pharmacological effect of compound X.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compound X is more effective at reducing migraine frequency than any currently available treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All patients who participated in the study had suffered from chronic migraines for at least one year prior to the trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The neurologist who conducted the study had no financial interest in the commercial development of compound X.

explanations.correct: The argument infers pharmacological effectiveness from patient-reported improvement. Negate B: the reduction was due to placebo effect, not compound X. The conclusion that compound X is effective collapses immediately. B is a necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Side effects concern safety and tolerability, not whether the observed reduction was caused by compound X. Out of scope for this causal inference.
explanations.B: Correct. The placebo/expectation alternative directly undermines the causal link between compound X and the reported improvement.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument concludes only that compound X is effective, not that it is superior to all alternatives. This is a sufficient-not-necessary trap.
explanations.D: Duration of prior migraine history is irrelevant to whether compound X caused the observed reduction. Shift in subject.
explanations.E: Financial interest concerns bias in reporting, not whether the compound itself was the causal agent. Out of scope.

difficultyReason: Economics stimulus with a structural gap between market data and a policy conclusion. Multiple close-cousin distractors test whether test-takers can identify the narrow bridge the argument truly needs.
stimulus: Economist: Over the past decade, the nations with the highest rates of economic growth have also had the lowest corporate tax rates among industrialized countries. Thus, reducing corporate tax rates is likely to stimulate significant economic growth in nations that currently have high corporate tax rates.
questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corporate tax revenue is the largest single source of government income in most industrialized nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The high-growth nations did not share some other feature, distinct from low corporate tax rates, that was responsible for their superior growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every industrialized nation that reduces its corporate tax rate will immediately experience faster economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nations with low corporate tax rates invest the resulting revenue savings in infrastructure projects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic growth rates are the most important measure of a nation's financial well-being.

explanations.correct: The economist infers causation from correlation. Negate B: the high-growth nations did share another feature responsible for growth. Then the correlation between low taxes and growth proves nothing about reducing taxes elsewhere. The argument collapses.
explanations.A: The share of revenue from corporate taxes is irrelevant to whether cutting those taxes drives growth. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out confounding variables, the key gap in any correlation-to-causation argument.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'every nation... immediately' exceeds what the argument concludes ('likely to stimulate'). Sufficient trap.
explanations.D: Infrastructure investment is an unrelated causal mechanism not invoked in the argument. Shift in subject.
explanations.E: Whether growth is the most important metric is irrelevant to the causal inference being drawn. Out of scope.

difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus. The conclusion depends on a link between current measurements and past conditions. One distractor is a close cousin that swaps subject scope.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: Core samples taken from the glacier show that atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were significantly lower three thousand years ago than they are today. Since the region's average temperature was also lower at that time, we can conclude that the current elevated carbon dioxide levels are a primary cause of the region's present higher temperatures.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No volcanic activity occurred in the region three thousand years ago that could have temporarily depressed CO₂ levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon dioxide levels in the glacier core samples accurately reflect the atmospheric CO₂ levels of three thousand years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's temperature and CO₂ levels have increased at the same rate over the past three thousand years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated carbon dioxide levels are the only factor that can cause a region's average temperature to rise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The glacier from which the core samples were taken has not significantly advanced or retreated in the past three thousand years.

explanations.correct: The entire argument rests on the glacier core data as a proxy for past atmospheric CO₂. Negate B: the core samples do not accurately reflect past atmospheric CO₂. Then the premise about lower CO₂ three thousand years ago is unsupported, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Volcanic activity is a possible confound for temperature, not for the CO₂ measurement accuracy the argument depends on. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument treats the glacier cores as reliable records of past atmospheric CO₂; without this, there is no evidence for the correlation that supports the conclusion.
explanations.C: Identical rates of increase are not required — only that CO₂ and temperature were both lower then and both higher now. Too strong.
explanations.D: Too strong — the conclusion says CO₂ is 'a primary cause,' not 'the only cause.' Universal language makes this a sufficient trap.
explanations.E: Glacier advance or retreat affects the physical mass of the glacier, not the chemical composition of trapped air bubbles. Shift in subject.

difficultyReason: Legal reasoning stimulus where a definitional gap exists between statutory language and the conclusion. Distractors include a reversed-direction trap and an out-of-scope trap.
stimulus: Attorney: The statute prohibits any person from operating a motor vehicle while impaired by any substance. My client was found asleep in the driver's seat of a parked car with the engine running. The prosecution contends that my client was operating a motor vehicle. However, since my client was asleep, she could not have been operating the vehicle, and so the statute does not apply.
questionStem: The attorney's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the statute was not intended to deter people from sleeping in running vehicles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a person who is asleep cannot perform the act of operating a vehicle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the client had a legitimate reason for sitting in the parked car with the engine running.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a vehicle with its engine running poses no traffic hazard when it is parked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the prosecution has not established that any substance caused the client's sleep.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'client was asleep' to 'client was not operating the vehicle.' This requires that being asleep precludes operating a vehicle. Negate B: a sleeping person can operate a vehicle (perhaps by having started it and left it running). Then the attorney's inference fails.
explanations.A: Legislative intent concerns statutory interpretation, not the logical connection the attorney draws between sleep and non-operation. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the bridge between 'asleep' and 'not operating,' the key gap in the attorney's argument.
explanations.C: The client's reason for being in the car is irrelevant to whether she was operating it. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Traffic hazard addresses policy rationale, not the definitional question of whether she was 'operating' the vehicle. Out of scope.
explanations.E: The attorney's argument rests on sleep negating operation, not on challenging the impairment element. This is a reversal — it addresses a different element of the statute.

difficultyReason: Technology stimulus. The argument infers a current system's reliability from past performance data. A temporal gap between past and present conditions is the key necessary assumption.
stimulus: Software engineer: Our automated trading platform has executed over two million transactions in the past three years without a single processing error. We are therefore confident that the platform will continue to operate without errors as transaction volume increases over the next year.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the engineer's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The automated trading platform was designed by engineers with at least ten years of experience in financial software.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No competing trading platform has achieved a comparable error-free record over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increase in transaction volume anticipated for the next year will not exceed the operational parameters under which the platform's error-free record was established.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Processing errors in automated trading platforms always result in significant financial losses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The platform has never been tested under simulated conditions of higher transaction volume.

explanations.correct: The argument extrapolates from past performance to future performance under increased volume. Negate C: the anticipated volume will exceed the parameters under which the platform performed error-free. Then the past record provides no basis for confidence about future performance. The conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Engineer credentials are irrelevant to whether future performance will match past performance. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Competitors' records are irrelevant to this platform's future reliability. Out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. This bridges past and future by ruling out the possibility that new conditions render past data inapplicable.
explanations.D: The consequence of errors is not required for the argument about whether errors will occur. Out of scope.
explanations.E: Simulation testing history doesn't affect the inference from actual past performance. This is a distractor that sounds relevant but shifts the evidentiary basis.

difficultyReason: History stimulus with a provenance-based inference. Multiple distractors are topically continuous but address different elements of the argument than the actual gap.
stimulus: Historian: This unsigned portrait, recently discovered in a private collection, was painted in the style of the Flemish master Jan van Eyck and uses a pigment blend found exclusively in his authenticated works. We can therefore conclude that van Eyck painted this portrait.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jan van Eyck painted more unsigned works than signed ones during his lifetime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other painter of van Eyck's era had access to or used the same pigment blend found in this portrait.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The portrait depicts a subject who was known to have sat for van Eyck on at least one occasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The private collection in which the portrait was found has a well-documented chain of ownership tracing to fifteenth-century Bruges.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Van Eyck's authenticated works are considered among the most valuable paintings of the Northern Renaissance.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the distinctive pigment blend as the key evidence. Negate B: another painter of van Eyck's era also used this pigment blend. Then the pigment no longer identifies the portrait as van Eyck's, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The ratio of signed to unsigned works is irrelevant to whether this particular portrait was painted by van Eyck. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. The argument requires the pigment blend to be uniquely attributable to van Eyck; without this, the evidence is not diagnostic.
explanations.C: The identity of the subject is not invoked as evidence in the argument. Shift in subject.
explanations.D: Provenance tracing to Bruges would strengthen the argument but is not a necessary assumption — the pigment and style evidence could stand independently. Too strong / out of scope.
explanations.E: The market value of van Eyck's work is entirely irrelevant to the attribution argument. Out of scope.

difficultyReason: Ethics stimulus with a normative gap between a factual premise and an evaluative conclusion. One distractor embodies the reversed-direction trap; another is a too-strong universal.
stimulus: Ethicist: A policy is just only if it distributes burdens and benefits in proportion to each individual's ability to bear them. The proposed carbon tax distributes its financial burden equally across all income levels. Therefore, the proposed carbon tax is not a just policy.
questionStem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A policy that distributes burdens in proportion to ability to bear them is always just.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The financial burden of the proposed carbon tax represents a greater proportional hardship for lower-income individuals than for higher-income individuals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon taxes are a less effective means of reducing emissions than direct regulatory mandates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No tax policy that distributes burdens equally across income levels can achieve its environmental objectives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The benefits of the carbon tax are distributed equally across all income levels as well.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'equal distribution across income levels' to 'not proportional to ability to bear.' This only works if equal dollar amounts impose unequal proportional hardship on different income levels. Negate B: an equal dollar burden is not a greater proportional hardship for lower-income individuals. Then equal distribution might be proportional, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.A: This is the converse of the first premise, not its logical entailment. Reversed-direction trap — the premise says just policies must distribute proportionally, not that proportional distribution is sufficient for justice.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the unstated bridge connecting 'equal across income levels' to 'not proportional to ability to bear.'
explanations.C: Comparative effectiveness of emissions-reduction tools is entirely outside the scope of this justice argument. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Too strong — introduces a universal about all equal-burden tax policies and their environmental objectives, neither of which is the argument's focus.
explanations.E: Benefit distribution was not invoked as part of the injustice argument. Shift in subject.

difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a synchronic-to-diachronic inferential gap. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed linguistic feature.
stimulus: Linguist: The word for 'fire' in six of the seven languages spoken in the Kareth Valley is derived from a common root. Languages typically borrow words for new concepts from neighboring tongues but retain indigenous terms for fundamental, long-established concepts. Since fire is a fundamental concept, these six languages almost certainly descended from a single common ancestor language.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The seventh language of the Kareth Valley did not descend from the same common ancestor as the other six.

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of the six languages borrowed the word for 'fire' from a single source language after these languages had already diverged from one another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All languages that share a common ancestor will retain identical words for fundamental concepts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Kareth Valley has been continuously inhabited for at least ten thousand years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The linguist analyzed written records of all six languages rather than relying solely on spoken forms.

explanations.correct: The argument infers common ancestry from a shared root word. But if the six languages borrowed 'fire' from one dominant language after diverging, they could share the root without sharing an ancestor. Negate B: the six languages did borrow the word from a single source after diverging. The shared root no longer evidences common ancestry, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: The seventh language's ancestry is a separate question; the argument only needs to establish common ancestry for the six. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out borrowing as an alternative explanation for the shared root, which is the key gap in the argument.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument requires only that these six share a root for 'fire,' not that all descendant languages always retain identical words. Sufficient trap.
explanations.D: Duration of habitation is not a premise in the argument and is not required for the shared-root inference. Out of scope.
explanations.E: The method of data collection (written vs. spoken) is not relevant to whether the shared root evidences common ancestry. Out of scope.

difficultyReason: Policy stimulus with a gap between stated program outcomes and the causal attribution. A close-cousin distractor shifts scope from program participants to the general population.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Participants in the city's subsidized job-training program showed a 34 percent increase in annual earnings two years after completing the program. The program costs the city $2,400 per participant. Since this earnings increase far exceeds the program's per-participant cost, the program represents a sound investment of public funds.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The job-training program is the primary reason participants experienced the increase in annual earnings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's overall unemployment rate declined during the two years following program completion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Participants in the program were, on average, earning below the city's median income before enrolling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city has sufficient funds to expand the program to serve twice as many participants annually.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No participant in the program subsequently moved out of the city within two years of completing it.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the participants' earnings increase as a return on the program's investment. Negate A: the program was not the primary reason for the earnings increase. Then the $2,400 cost cannot be credited with producing the earnings gain, and the investment-worthiness conclusion fails.
explanations.A: Correct. The cost-benefit comparison only holds if the program, not some other factor, caused the earnings increase.
explanations.B: City-wide unemployment trends could explain participant outcomes but the argument doesn't require ruling this in — it requires ruling it out as the cause. B is out of scope as stated; A captures the necessary causal assumption more precisely.
explanations.C: Pre-program income level of participants is irrelevant to whether the program caused the post-program earnings increase. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Expansion capacity concerns future policy, not whether the current program is a sound investment. Out of scope.
explanations.E: Participants who move away still experienced the earnings increase; geographic mobility does not sever the causal claim. Shift in subject.

difficultyReason: Arts stimulus with an inferential gap between physical evidence about a manuscript and a conclusion about authorial intent. Distractors include a too-strong universal and an out-of-scope trap about manuscript value.
stimulus: Music historian: The earliest surviving manuscript of this symphony contains numerous passages crossed out and rewritten in the same hand as the rest of the score. Composers of this period routinely completed a full draft before preparing a clean final copy. The crossed-out passages therefore represent the composer's deliberate revisions, not copying errors.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The surviving manuscript is a draft copy rather than the clean final copy the composer prepared for performance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every composer of this period made extensive revisions before completing a final copy of a symphony.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The crossed-out passages contain musical ideas that the composer later incorporated into other works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The manuscript was stored under conditions that prevented deterioration of the ink over time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The composer did not employ a copyist to transcribe any portion of the manuscript.

explanations.correct: The argument relies on the premise that composers completed a full draft before a clean copy, and concludes the cross-outs are intentional revisions. This only works if the manuscript is a draft — if it is the clean final copy, cross-outs would more likely be errors. Negate A: the manuscript is the clean final copy, not a draft. Then the premise about drafting practice no longer supports the conclusion that cross-outs are deliberate revisions.
explanations.A: Correct. The drafting-practice premise is only relevant if this manuscript is a draft; the argument assumes this without stating it.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'every composer' is a universal that exceeds what the argument needs. The argument requires only that this composer (or composers of this period generally) followed this practice. Sufficient trap.
explanations.C: Whether crossed-out ideas appeared elsewhere is irrelevant to whether they were deliberate revisions or errors. Out of scope.
explanations.D: Ink preservation concerns the legibility of the manuscript, not the intentionality of the cross-outs. Out of scope.
explanations.E: A copyist's involvement would be relevant if the cross-outs might be in a different hand, but the stimulus already establishes they are in the same hand as the rest of the score. This distractor is rendered moot by information already in the stimulus.
